canonical_question: What should I understand about sends versus inserts, and why does it matter in Logic Pro?
clarification_questions: Is the effect supposed to transform the whole source or add a parallel layer?
Which tracks or returns are involved, and what should stay unchanged?
Is the goal shared audio processing, parallel wet processing, linked control, or organization only?
competing_hypotheses: The current insert may be correct; a shared aux may give better independent control; the problem may only be level mismatch.
The routing itself may be correct and the perceived problem may be level, processing, automation, solo behavior, or arrangement context.
direct_answer: An insert processes the whole channel in series; a send splits off a parallel copy to a bus and aux. Focus on the routing concept before touching processing. A safe first test is: Duplicate or preserve the track, compare one effect as an insert against the same effect on a 100% wet aux, and level-match the result. Listen for whether the effect feels integrated into the source or behaves better as a separately controlled layer. The main risk is creating duplicate dry signal or judging the louder route as better.
evidence_needed: The exact Logic version and the visible Output, Send, Bus, Aux, Group, Stack, and VCA assignments involved.
A preserved baseline and one controlled mute/bypass/routing test with no unrelated changes.
Source and return meters, audible dry/wet behavior, and whether the same result occurs in the complete mix and in mono where relevant.
The user’s report of what changed, stayed unchanged, or became less clear after the test.
key_distinction: An insert processes the whole channel in series; a send splits off a parallel copy to a bus and aux.
limitations: A routing label, meter, solo state, or waveform does not by itself prove the musical result.
Professional and community routing practices are context-bound and may disagree.
